title: AI Agents Are Thirsty for Power
gist: Wired's Power Play column argues the shift from simple chatbot queries to autonomous, self-re-prompting AI agents (not consumer chatbot use) is the real driver of the data center buildout, since agentic workloads are decoupled from human usage caps and can expand near-limitlessly as tasks grow more complex.

themes.theme: Agents, not chatbots, are driving the power buildout

insights.claim: The core driver of hyperscaler data center construction is the shift from single-query chatbot interactions to autonomous AI agents that generate hundreds of self-issued sub-prompts to complete a task, which multiplies compute and energy consumption per user request far beyond simple chatbot use.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Investors sizing data center capex and power demand should model agentic workload growth (recursive self-prompting), not chatbot query volume, as the key demand driver going forward.
insights.quote: Rather than asking an AI chatbot a simple question and answer, these agents can give themselves hundreds of small prompts based on a user's original question.
insights.locator: Quote from Maxwell Zeff, Model Behavior newsletter writer

insights.claim: Unlike other technology growth areas that are capped by the number of human users (e.g., people driving cars or streaming Netflix), agentic AI compute demand is decoupled from user counts, and AI leaders are explicitly working toward business models with 'one employee' supervising hundreds or thousands of background AI agents.
insights.speaker: Boris Gamazaychikov (Sustainable AI), via Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A framework for why AI power demand could scale without historical usage ceilings: agent fan-out per user is an open-ended multiplier, making long-run electricity demand forecasts structurally different from past compute cycles.
insights.quote: In other technological growth areas, we're constrained by how many people are driving a car or streaming Netflix... Now, this stuff is kind of decoupled from users—and if you listen to AI leaders, I think that's what they want. They're talking about unicorns that have one employee.

insights.claim: The technology being trained in data centers currently under proposal and construction will not be deployed for three to five years, and will look categorically different from today's chatbot interfaces, implying today's buildout is being sized for a future agentic paradigm rather than current-generation products.
insights.speaker: Boris Gamazaychikov, via Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Current data center capex should be read as a forward bet on a 3-5 year-out agentic AI paradigm shift, meaning near-term utilization/ROI metrics may understate the strategic rationale behind hyperscaler spending.
insights.quote: The technology that's going to be trained by the data centers that are being proposed and built right now is three to five years away... It's going to be a very different flavor than just the chatbot window.
insights.locator: Quote from Boris Gamazaychikov, near end of column

insights.claim: OpenAI announced a swarm of more than 10,000 AI agents sending 2.7 million messages that solved a longstanding math problem, an effort Wired's Molly Taft estimates burned through 'tens of millions of dollars' worth' of compute/energy, though mathematicians disputed the validity of OpenAI's claims about the achievement.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A single agentic research stunt costing tens of millions in compute illustrates how expensive and energy-intensive frontier-lab agent swarms already are, and how disputed their headline claims can be, warranting skepticism of AI labs' self-reported capability milestones.
insights.quote: OpenAI announced that a swarm of more than 10,000 agents sending 2.7 million messages had solved a longstanding math problem. (Mathematicians pushed back on the company's claims.)

insights.claim: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has publicly framed AI water usage in trivializing terms, claiming a single ChatGPT query's water footprint is equivalent to roughly 1/38,000th of the water needed to grow one almond, a calculation that has been disputed and that Taft frames as understating the true resource footprint once agentic use is included.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft (citing Sam Altman)
insights.so_what: Frontier AI labs' public environmental-impact framing (per-query, almond-equivalent comparisons) is a rhetorical strategy that may materially understate real footprint once always-on agent workloads are counted, a due-diligence flag for ESG-focused investors.
insights.quote: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman claimed that the water use needed to harvest a single almond amounted to 38,000 ChatGPT queries... 'The people that are scarfing down 12 almonds at a time don't feel like they're doing something horrible from a water perspective for the most part.'

insights.claim: There is little reliable public data on AI agent energy use, and even independent third-party research groups working to quantify it (e.g., Sustainable AI) describe existing outside estimates as based on outdated methodology, reflecting how opaque AI companies remain about disclosing emissions and energy metrics.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft (citing Boris Gamazaychikov)
insights.so_what: The absence of standardized, verified agent-energy disclosure is a research and regulatory gap; expect emerging third-party estimates (Sustainable AI's forthcoming research) to become a reference point investors and regulators start citing.
insights.quote: There's a major dearth of information around the energy use of agents, whose tasks can range from simple jobs to a full day of autonomous coding involving a team of parallel 'helper' agents.
insights.locator: Paragraph on dearth of agent energy information

insights.claim: Climate scientist Zeke Hausfather calculated that his own daily AI use, which leans heavily on agents (largely via Claude), may consume more energy than running two refrigerators, though he called this personally not world-ending while noting it still represents a net-new source of emissions at a time when climate goals are falling behind.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft (citing Zeke Hausfather)
insights.so_what: A credible independent, if rough, benchmark (2 refrigerators/day for a heavy agentic user) gives investors a tangible per-user energy proxy to sanity-check AI power-demand growth assumptions as agent adoption scales beyond power users.
insights.quote: He used a variety of different sources to work out that his average daily Claude session may consume more than the energy needed to power two refrigerators.
insights.locator: Paragraph on Zeke Hausfather's blog post

themes.theme: Mass consumer rollout of personal agents

insights.claim: Meta rolled out a personal AI agent called Muse, described in a company press release as built to work for billions of people worldwide, that maintains a dedicated cloud computer for each user which keeps operating even while the user is offline, with plans to integrate it with Meta's AI glasses later in 2026.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: A billions-of-users-scale always-on personal agent product from Meta represents a step-change in aggregate compute/energy demand versus on-demand chatbot queries, since each user's agent runs continuously rather than only when prompted.
insights.quote: Meta rolled out a personal AI agent that, the company said in a press release, is 'built to work for billions of people worldwide.' Dubbed Muse, Meta trumpeted that it will maintain a 'dedicated computer in the cloud' for each user that would work even when the user is offline.

insights.claim: The Hyperion data center project in Louisiana will be powered by 10 natural gas plants, illustrating the scale of new fossil-fuel generation being built specifically to support AI data center capacity.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that hyperscale AI buildout is directly driving new natural-gas generation capacity, relevant to energy-sector investors tracking gas-plant order books tied to AI demand rather than traditional grid growth.
insights.quote: It explains the massive scale of some of the data centers they're building—like the Hyperion project in Louisiana, which will be powered by 10 natural gas plants.
insights.locator: Paragraph on Meta's Muse and Hyperion

themes.theme: Small modular reactors as a data center power solution

insights.claim: Despite startup and utility interest in small modular reactors (SMRs) as carbon-free power for data centers, no SMRs are operating commercially in the US and only one model has been licensed for sale, despite decades of development, with the Trump administration running a Department of Energy pilot for 11 SMR startups to hit a key milestone in 2026 (at least a handful have succeeded so far).
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: SMRs remain commercially unproven at scale despite policy support, meaning data center developers cannot rely on them for near-term power and are instead defaulting to gas turbines now — a timing gap relevant to nuclear-supply-chain and gas-turbine investment theses alike.
insights.quote: No small modular reactors are operating commercially in the US, and just one model has been licensed for sale, despite decades of development.
insights.locator: What You're Asking section, SMR question

insights.claim: Because SMRs remain years away from commercial maturity, many data center developers are not waiting and are instead installing gas turbines now to meet near-term power needs.
insights.speaker: Molly Taft
insights.so_what: This confirms gas turbine manufacturers are the near-term beneficiaries of data center power demand while nuclear SMR commercialization lags, an important sequencing signal for energy-equipment order flow.
insights.quote: Many data center developers don't want to wait years for these companies to prove themselves, so they're installing gas turbines now. In other words, they're not waiting for utopia to come around.
insights.locator: What You're Asking section, closing lines
